title: Level 1 – Qualified Nurse
subtitle: Child Health Nursing
intro: Welcome to GNPS Program 7 - Caring for Children and Families. Paediatric nursing requires nurses to understand that infants, children and adolescents are not simply smaller adults. Their anatomy, physiology, communication, development, medication needs and responses to illness differ across age groups. This level is designed around the paediatric capabilities expected within national nursing education programs and by nursing regulatory bodies across different countries. It develops the essential knowledge, assessment skills and professional behaviours required to provide safe, developmentally appropriate and family-centred care. Throughout this level you will strengthen your ability to: Apply paediatric nursing principles across infancy, childhood and adolescence Assess physical growth and developmental milestones Use age-appropriate communication and pain-assessment methods Recognise normal and abnormal paediatric vital signs Provide safe care for common respiratory, cardiac, gastrointestinal and neurological conditions Calculate and administer medicines safely using weight-based principles Assess hydration, nutrition and growth Promote injury prevention and child wellbeing Work respectfully with parents, carers and families Children may deteriorate rapidly and may not describe symptoms clearly. A change in behaviour, reduced feeding, grunting, lethargy or fewer wet nappies may be an early sign of serious illness. Safe paediatric nursing depends on careful observation, developmental knowledge and early action. By the end of Level 1, you should be able to assess and care for children across different age groups, recognise common childhood illness and deterioration, and communicate effectively with children and families within your scope of practice.

content.text: Growth and development influence how children communicate, respond to illness, understand procedures and participate in care. Paediatric nurses must adapt assessment and intervention to developmental stage while recognising parents and carers as important partners.
Learning outcomes
Describe growth and development across paediatric age groups Recognise key developmental milestones
Use age-appropriate play and communication Explain the principles of family-centred care

Growth and Development Infants, toddlers, preschool children, school-age children and adolescents have different physical, cognitive, language and psychosocial needs. Development should be considered alongside chronological age and individual ability.

Developmental Milestones Milestones provide guidance about expected motor, language, social and cognitive progress. Variation occurs, but persistent delay or loss of previously acquired skills requires further assessment.

Communication and Play Simple language, demonstration, distraction, therapeutic play and offering limited choices can reduce fear. Adolescents require privacy, respect and opportunities to speak independently where appropriate.

Family-Centred Care Parents and carers usually know the child's normal behaviour best. Their observations should be valued, and they should be involved in decisions, comfort and care according to the child's needs and family preferences.

A four-year-old is frightened before a blood test. The nurse uses a doll to demonstrate the procedure, explains it in simple language and allows the child to choose which arm to present. The parent remains nearby for reassurance. Developmentally appropriate preparation reduces fear and improves cooperation.
Key learning points
Adapt communication to developmental stage Use play as a clinical communication tool
Recognise developmental delay or regression Treat families as partners in care

sections.title: Paediatric Assessment and Recognition of Deterioration

content.text: Paediatric assessment requires attention to age-specific vital signs, behaviour, breathing, circulation, hydration and neurological status. Children may compensate for illness before deteriorating suddenly, making early recognition essential.
Learning outcomes
Perform a systematic paediatric assessment Use age-appropriate pain assessment tools
Recognise respiratory distress and dehydration Identify early signs of paediatric deterioration

Observation First Before touching the child, observe appearance, interaction, breathing, colour, posture and response to the caregiver. A quiet, floppy or poorly responsive child may be seriously unwell.
Vital Signs and Pain Normal heart rate, respiratory rate and blood pressure vary with age. Pain tools such as FLACC, Wong-Baker and CRIES support assessment when verbal reporting is limited.
Airway and Breathing Children have smaller airways and higher oxygen demands. Stridor, grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, poor air entry or central cyanosis require urgent attention.

Hydration and Neurological Status Tears, mucous membranes, fontanel tension, capillary refill, urine output and activity help assess hydration. Irritability, lethargy, seizures or altered consciousness may indicate serious illness.

An infant with bronchiolitis becomes less interested in feeding and quieter than earlier. The nurse notes nasal flaring, chest retractions and reduced wet nappies. The change in behaviour and breathing is recognised as deterioration, and urgent review is requested.
Key learning points
Observe behaviour before beginning the examination Use age-specific vital-sign ranges
Treat respiratory distress as a priority Recognise poor feeding and reduced urine output as important cues

sections.title: Nursing Care for Common Childhood Conditions

content.text: Children commonly require nursing care for respiratory, cardiac, gastrointestinal, neurological and endocrine conditions. Safe care combines early recognition, evidence-based intervention and support for the child and family.
Learning outcomes
Describe priority care for common childhood illnesses Recognise red-flag symptoms
Monitor response to treatment Support children and families during acute illness

Respiratory Conditions Asthma, bronchiolitis, croup, pneumonia and cystic fibrosis may impair breathing. Nursing care includes airway assessment, positioning, oxygen and inhaled treatment as prescribed, hydration and monitoring for fatigue.
Cardiac Conditions Congenital heart disease and heart failure may present with poor feeding, sweating, cyanosis, reduced growth or respiratory difficulty. Activity and feeding may need to be paced.

Gastrointestinal Conditions Gastroenteritis and dehydration are common, while bilious vomiting, currant-jelly stool, severe abdominal pain or a distended abdomen may indicate urgent surgical conditions.

Neurological and Endocrine Conditions Seizures, meningitis, type 1 diabetes and diabetic ketoacidosis require rapid assessment. Fever with a non-blanching rash, bulging fontanel, altered consciousness or deep breathing requires urgent action.

A school-age child with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing and increasing drowsiness. The nurse checks glucose and ketones, recognises possible diabetic ketoacidosis and activates urgent medical management.
Key learning points
Know the red flags associated with common conditions Monitor breathing, hydration and consciousness closely
Escalate bilious vomiting, non-blanching rash or altered consciousness Support both the child and family during illness

sections.title: Medication Safety, Nutrition and Child Protection

content.text: Paediatric medication doses are commonly based on weight, and small errors can cause serious harm. Nutrition, hydration and safety are also central because children depend on adults for care and protection.
Learning outcomes
Apply weight-based medication principles Assess nutrition and hydration
Promote age-appropriate injury prevention Recognise possible abuse or neglect

Medication Safety The child's current weight in kilograms should be confirmed. Dose, concentration, route and maximum safe dose must be checked carefully. Paediatric medicines often require independent verification.
Nutrition and Growth Feeding needs change from infancy to adolescence. Growth charts, dietary history and feeding observation help identify undernutrition, obesity or feeding difficulty.
Injury Prevention Safe sleep, car restraints, drowning prevention, poison storage, burn prevention and sport safety should be tailored to age and development.

Safeguarding Injuries inconsistent with the explanation, unusual bruising patterns, delayed presentation, poor hygiene, fearfulness or concerning caregiver behaviour may indicate abuse or neglect. Nurses must follow legal and organisational reporting requirements.

A toddler is prescribed a medicine based on weight. The nurse discovers that the recorded weight was entered in pounds rather than kilograms. Administration is paused, the child is reweighed and the dose is recalculated. The correction prevents a potentially serious overdose.
Key learning points
Use kilograms for paediatric calculations Double-check high-risk and weight-based doses
Include injury prevention in family education Report safeguarding concerns through approved pathways

End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 7 - Level 1, you have developed the foundational knowledge and practical skills required to assess children, understand growth and development, manage common childhood illness and promote safety. These capabilities prepare you for Level 2 - International Qualified Nurse, where the focus expands to complex paediatric care, international standards and safeguarding.
